title: Before You Teach a Single Prompt, Say What You Believe
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Before deploying AI in schools, educational leaders must first publicly declare what they believe about AI and children—not a policy document full of rules, but a brief statement of purpose the whole community can read, quote, and hold leadership accountable to. The cost of skipping this step is illustrated vividly by New York City's 2023 ChatGPT ban: the district spent four months enforcing a fear-driven position before reversing course, teaching its community that leadership didn't know what it believed—a credibility wound that outlasted both the ban and the reversal. Peninsula School District outside Tacoma did the opposite: by publishing human-centered AI principles before the tools arrived, they could evaluate every new tool against pre-existing values rather than scrambling to respond to each new pressure. The vacuum a school creates by saying nothing about AI is not neutrality—it fills with whatever anxiety is loudest in the community. Los Angeles Unified's failed AI chatbot purchase illustrates the risk from the other direction: buying a tool without a stated belief leaves no story to tell when the product fails. A belief statement short enough to remember and honest enough to defend is the essential first step of any human-first AI framework, because its real purpose is building the trust that makes every subsequent decision easier.
points: The first step in any AI rollout is not a tool, training, or policy—it is a public statement of belief that the whole community can read, explaining what the school believes about AI and children and why it is teaching what it teaches.

New York City's four-month ban-and-reversal on ChatGPT illustrates the price of policy without a declared why: the rules changed twice, the belief was never stated once, and the credibility damage outlasted both decisions.

Peninsula School District's human-centered AI principles, published before generative AI arrived, demonstrate what early public commitment buys—not a head start on software, but a head start on trust that allows new tools to be evaluated against pre-existing values.

When a school says nothing, it doesn't create neutrality; it creates a vacuum that fills with the loudest available anxiety—and Common Sense Media research found that most teenagers were already using generative AI while most of their parents had no idea.

A belief statement works where policy fails because it names the purpose behind the rules: parents who understand the why extend grace when a lesson is imperfect; parents who only see the what read every misstep as evidence there was never a plan.
quotes: But here is what I’ve watched happen in schools that skip this step. A teacher tries something with AI, a parent hears about it secondhand, and by the time the question reaches the principal’s office it has curdled into suspicion: why is my child using this, what happened to real learning, who decided this.

the decision had been driven by fear, by knee-jerk caution, rather than by any considered belief about what students actually needed. Think about what those four months cost. Not just the instructional time. The credibility.

When ChatGPT arrived and districts everywhere were whipsawing between panic and paralysis, Peninsula didn’t have to scramble. The belief was already on the record. The community had already read it. New tools could be evaluated against a standard that existed before the tools did. That is what being early actually buys you — not a head start on software, but a head start on trust.
When a school says nothing, it doesn’t create neutrality. It creates a vacuum, and vacuums fill with the loudest available anxiety.

A district that starts with what to buy instead of what it believes has no standard to buy against, and no story to tell its community when the product stumbles. The tool was the strategy. When the tool died, so did the strategy.

we are preparing students to understand AI and stand on their own with it once they leave us. Not to master one particular app — the apps will be unrecognizable in five years anyway. To carry judgment into a world that will be saturated with these tools long after graduation.

A policy tells people what the rules are. A belief tells them why the rules exist — and a parent who understands the why will extend you grace when a lesson is imperfect, because they trust the direction.
